live.name: GOLD HARVEST
live.headline: GOLD HARVEST: a threat actor tracked under several names
live.in_short: The catalogue lists GOLD HARVEST under five other names and names three remote-access tools tied to it. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: The catalogue record, sourced to Secureworks, tracks the actor as GOLD HARVEST.
The same record lists these aliases: Octo Tempest, Roasted 0ktapus, Scatter Swine, Scattered Spider and UNC3944.
The record lists three tools: AnyDesk, ConnectWise Control and Logmein.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: GOLD HARVEST
next.headline: GOLD HARVEST (Scattered Spider): a social-engineering extortion crew that goes after help desks
next.in_short: GOLD HARVEST is Secureworks' name for the group also tracked as Scattered Spider. Vendors describe a financially motivated actor that talks its way past help desks and MFA, often to steal data and sometimes to deploy ransomware.

sentences.t: GOLD HARVEST is Secureworks' name for a group also tracked as Scattered Spider, Octo Tempest, UNC3944, Scatter Swine and Roasted 0ktapus.
CrowdStrike describes Scattered Spider as a prolific eCrime actor that has run financially motivated activity since early 2022.
Check Point Research, drawing on public intelligence, says the group is composed mainly of young people aged 19 to 22 from the US and UK.
ReliaQuest describes it as a financially motivated gang associated with the wider hacking collective known as The Com.
Trustwave SpiderLabs reads the Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters brand, which borrows the Scattered Spider, ShinyHunters and LAPSUS$ names, as a situational alliance and not a formal merger.
EclecticIQ assesses that ShinyHunters very likely relies on members of Scattered Spider and The Com to carry out voice phishing.
CrowdStrike says early campaigns reportedly hit customer relationship management and business-process outsourcing firms, plus telecommunications and technology companies.
ReliaQuest reports that 70% of the group's targets sit in technology, finance and retail trade.

Halcyon says the group compromises call centers and other outsourcing providers to reach many clients at once. Halcyon assesses that attacks on UK retail and US insurance likely began, at least in part, this way.
Check Point Research says the group is broadening its scope to aviation alongside enterprise environments.
Mandiant's M-Trends 2026 says UNC3944 targets IT help desks to get around multifactor authentication.
ReliaQuest says the group relies on phishing, vishing and help-desk impersonation. It uses the Evilginx phishing framework and typosquatted domains to bypass MFA.
Check Point Research lists SIM swapping, MFA fatigue and tricking employees into installing remote access tools among the group's methods.
Halcyon says the group has consistently used insider recruitment. It likely enrolled new MFA tokens to keep access.
The catalogue record lists AnyDesk, ConnectWise Control and Logmein among the group's tools.
ReliaQuest says the group has allied with ransomware operators ALPHV, RansomHub and DragonForce. Halcyon says it has been linked to Akira, Play, Qilin and DragonForce payloads.
Halcyon says encryption is typically an escalation step and not the first goal, with data-first extortion the broader model.
Sygnia names Scattered Spider among the groups that attack VMware ESXi virtualization environments.
BleepingComputer's report says that in September 2023 the group breached MGM Resorts by impersonating an employee, then encrypted over 100 VMware ESXi hypervisors with BlackCat ransomware.
ReliaQuest says a May 2025 wave of attacks hit UK retailers including Marks & Spencer, Co-op and Harrods. It adds that nothing definitive has tied those incidents to Scattered Spider.
After Aflac disclosed a breach in June 2025, a spokesperson could not name a group. The report says the breach shows all the signs of a Scattered Spider attack.

Check Point Research found about 500 domains that follow the group's naming patterns. It says not all are confirmed malicious. It adds that the link to airline attacks rests on media reports and advisories.

Rapid7 investigated an April 2026 intrusion that began with a Microsoft Teams message from a fake IT Support account. It says the approach mirrors tradecraft seen in Octo Tempest-style campaigns, and does not call it a confirmed link.
Treat help-desk password and MFA reset requests as high-risk. Confirm the caller through a second, known channel before acting.
Check outsourced support providers and third-party staff with the same care as your own.
